---
title: "Quiz: least-squares unmixing"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A pixel with $N$ channel values is $\mathbf y \approx M\mathbf a$, with the $K$ component spectra as the columns of $M$ ($N > K$); least squares gives $\hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y$, $M^+ = (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top$.

---

**Q1.** Why can't you simply invert $M$ when there are 16 channels and 4 dyes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What shape is $M$? How many equations per pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$M$ is $16 \times 4$: not square, no inverse. Each pixel gives 16 equations for 4 unknowns; with noise they cannot all hold. Least squares takes the 4 abundances whose mixture is **closest** to the measured spectrum.
:::

---

**Q2.** Geometrically, what is the least-squares fit $M\hat{\mathbf a}$ of a pixel, and what is the residual?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of 3 channels and 2 dyes: the set of all mixtures is a plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The fit is the **orthogonal projection** of the pixel onto the column space of $M$ (all mixtures of the spectra): the nearest explainable spectrum. The residual is the perpendicular part, $\mathbf y - M\hat{\mathbf a}$, orthogonal to every component spectrum.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is unmixing a $512 \times 512$ image with 32 channels cheap, even though every pixel needs its own least-squares fit?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does $M^+$ depend on?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$M^+$ depends only on the reference spectra, not on the pixel: compute it once ($K \times 32$), then every pixel's abundances are one small matrix–vector product, $\hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y$. The whole image is one matrix product $M^+Y$.
:::

---

**Q4.** After unmixing, the residual map is at the noise level everywhere except in the cytoplasm, where it is clearly higher. What would you suspect, and how would you test it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The residual is what no combination of your reference spectra can explain.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A component is missing from $M$, present in the cytoplasm only: typically **autofluorescence** (or an unexpected dye, or an offset). Look at the residual spectrum of those pixels, add a spectrum of that shape as an extra column (from an unstained control, for example) and check that the residual drops to the noise level.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two dyes have nearly the same spectrum. Which is better determined: the sum of their abundances or the difference? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the measured spectrum if you add a little of dye 1 and remove the same amount of dye 2?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The **sum**. Trading dye 1 for dye 2 hardly changes the measured spectrum, so the data cannot pin down the difference: noise moves it a lot. The total amount of light, and hence the sum, is well measured. In the math: $M^\top M$ has a small eigenvalue with eigenvector $\approx (1, -1)$.
:::

---

**Q6.** A colleague says "with 32 channels instead of 8 we can separate any two dyes". Is that right?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Do finer bins create new photons? Do they change the shapes?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Finer bins over the same range sample the shapes better and help a little (in the demo, noise × 5.7 → 4.7 for dyes 6 nm apart), but they add no photons, and two **identical** shapes stay inseparable however finely you sample them ($\kappa = \infty$). What helps more: dyes further apart, more photons.
:::

---

**Q7.** In a photon-starved image, why give a channel with 4 expected counts more weight than one with 400?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For Poisson counts the variance equals the mean.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The channel with 400 counts has variance 400 (sd 20); the one with 4 counts has variance 4 (sd 2). In absolute terms the dim channel's error is ten times smaller, so it deserves more weight: weighted least squares uses $w_c = 1/\text{expected count}$. (In relative terms the dim channel is noisier: 50 % against 5 %.)
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that $P = M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top$ satisfies $P^2 = P$. What does that mean for a pixel that is already a perfect mixture?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply out; the middle $M^\top M$ cancels one inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$P^2 = M(M^\top M)^{-1}(M^\top M)(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top = M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top = P$. Projecting twice changes nothing: a pixel that already lies in the column space, $\mathbf y = M\mathbf a$, has $P\mathbf y = \mathbf y$, its abundances are recovered exactly and its residual is zero.
:::
